metadata.title: What Separates AVGO From Its Peers Right Now

content.text:
This chip giant's profits are near the top of its class, but its stock performance is stuck in the middle of the pack. Has the market correctly spotted a flaw in the growth story?
Broadcom (AVGO) designs the high-end custom silicon that powers AI for tech giants and sells the critical infrastructure software that runs corporate data centers. After a year where its stock returned +35%, outperforming the S&P 500, it would seem the market is rewarding a top-tier operator. But a closer look at its competitive group reveals a sharp mismatch. Broadcom's profitability ranks near the top of its peer group, yet its stock performance and growth sit firmly in the middle. Has the market correctly identified a risk that its stellar margins can't overcome, or is this a case of performance yet to catch up with fundamentals?
How does Broadcom actually rank against its rivals? When lined up against its peers, Broadcom's operational strength is clear. Its operating margin is the second highest in the group, trailing only NVIDIA's 64%. This is a business that converts revenue into profit with formidable efficiency. Yet, the market appears unimpressed. The stock's +35% one-year return ranks just fourth out of six, lagging far behind the +186% posted by Marvell Technology and AMD's +176%.
The disconnect extends to growth and valuation. Broadcom's revenue grew 32% over the last twelve months, another fourth-place finish. Despite this mid-pack growth, the stock trades at 67.7 times earnings, the third-highest multiple in the group. Investors are paying a premium price for a company whose growth and stock returns are, so far, decidedly average for its cohort.
Is the market paying for a future that hasn't arrived? The market's gaze is fixed on one thing: artificial intelligence. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue hit a record $10.8 billion in its most recent quarter, and management expects that to accelerate to $16 billion in the next. This explosive demand is driven by a handful of core customers building out large AI infrastructure. The company's bookings for AI chips were over $30 billion in a single quarter, giving it visibility on orders that management says "runs all the way to 2028 right now." This focus on long-term AI partnerships suggests a strategic shift. Indeed, some analysis indicates Broadcom no longer sells itself as a chip cycle story.
